title: How Bob Barr Can Mainstream the Marijuana Issue. He Should Talk about The Dutch Experience As Concrete Proof that Cannabis Prohibition Is A Counterproductive Fraud.

Posted May 28, 2008 

Analysis (and free political advice) by Richard Cowan 

See 

Kubby Narrowly Misses Libertarian VP Slot. Will Play Key Role In Keeping Party Together Under Barr. Mainstreaming Marijuana Issues.

Whatever he may choose to call it, Bob Barr’s campaign strategy will be to “mainstream” the Libertarian Party. But how can he do this and still differentiate the LP from the duopoly – and not alienate the LP’s hardcore base? 

It will be easy for him to join both civil libertarians and many traditional conservatives in opposition to the excesses of the Bush Administration’s so-called “War on Terror” – such as the Patriot Act, and Iraqi fiasco. 

Also, because the Republicans always use libertarian rhetoric on economic issues, and “Big Government” in general, it will be even easier to sound mainstream there. 

However, precisely because these positions are already well-established in the mainstream, what would the LP candidates really be bringing to the campaign? Why should anyone bother with this new “mainstream” party? 

Of course, there is always what the libertarian writer, Bill Steigerwald called “the elephant in the room” in a recent interview with Barr. 

Steigerwald: What is your position on the war on drugs, which has always been the elephant in the room that nobody running for president has dared to talk about for the last 30 or 40 years? It's been a continuing war against the rights and liberties of Americans, yet no one touches it. 

Barr: We do need to start addressing it. I do not think that the American people are ready to embrace the notion that there ought to be across-the board legalization of drugs. But I do think we need to begin rolling back the massive government power structure that has been built up pursuant to the war on drugs, which has not proved to be a success, certainly. Therefore, I think we need to certainly respect states rights and decisions by the people in an area such as medicinal marijuana. If the people of California, for example, decide that there is an appropriate place for the use of marijuana for medicinal purposes and they pass a law to that affect, that ought to be respected by the federal government. In other words, I think we can start this process of vesting the power to decide what people want to do with their own lives as long as they don't endanger anyone else by at least beginning to devolve power from the federal government to the states. That would be an important first step. 

Bluntly, that is not the sort of answer that will get the public’s attention, much less rally the LP troops. The fact is that the American people have long since started “addressing” these issues. Only the leaders lag behind. Medical marijuana is supported by an overwhelming majority of Americans, most of whom also oppose arresting marijuana users.

See 

The Evil Idiocy of the Republican National Committee. Attacking Obama For Not Attacking the Sick and Dying. McCain Means Four More Years. 

and links 

In fairness to Barr, he spoke out more forcefully against the Drug War at the LP Convention, and his running mate, Wayne Root, was even more emphatic in his opposition to it. Nonetheless, if Barr’s mainstreamed LP is to get itself noticed, and actually try to lead the American people back to our traditional freedoms, we will need to do more than “start addressing” the marijuana issues. 

Obviously, Barr is right in saying that it must start by letting the states set their own medical marijuana policies. Under the American system, that is almost all that the President can do unilaterally – by calling off the DEA’s raids on medical growers and suppliers. However, that is what Barack Obama has said would be his policy, and it is certainly not the most that the LP’s Presidential candidate can talk about. 

I think that the most “mainstream” way that the LP candidates – or any others – can advance the marijuana issue is to point at the Dutch experience. For more than 30 years the Dutch have tolerated technically illegal marijuana sales – not just in Amsterdam, but in virtually all of the Dutch cities – and their rate of marijuana use, and hard drug use, is far below the American, Canadian, or British levels. 

See 

Tale of Two Countries, The Netherlands and Mexico, Regulation Versus Violence. Dutch Cannabis Smokers To Go “American”? When Will the Murders Cross Our Border? 

For mainstreaming the issue, it has to be emphasized that one reason the Dutch hard drug use rate is much lower than in many prohibitionist countries is that “legalizing” retail marijuana sales separates it from the hard drug market. When the Dutch buy their marijuana, no one will try to sell them hard drugs. They call it “separating the markets.” That will be easy for everyone to understand. 

Citing the practical Dutch success story takes the argument into the mainstream; this is not some hippie anarchist’s dream, and it also obviates the so-called “latest research” on marijuana, which always purports to show some dire effect of marijuana that has somehow gone heretofore unnoticed for the last 5,000 years. 

See 

Annotated NORML Weekly News for February 7, 2008; NORML Responds to “Latest Research”. Cannabinoids Kill Cancer. Noting Obama’s Retreat. 

The point is simply that marijuana prohibition is not just a failure; it is actually a counterproductive fraud, making the “drug problem” worse. 

See 

The Chaos of Cannabis Prohibition In France, DEAland and Latin America. More Proof That It Is A Counterproductive Fraud.

Barr will also quickly find that citing the Dutch experience will have another advantage in debating the issues: Lying about the Dutch has long been a basic part of prohibitionist propaganda, and these lies are easily debunked by citing readily available data.

See 

Drug Czar Uses Foreign Affairs Magazine Article For Anti-Dutch Propaganda, Elevating The Lying To Official Status. Analysis By Richard Cowan 

and links 

Americans are increasingly aware of – and outraged by – the lies that were told to get us into the Iraq War, but these pale in comparison with the lies told to maintain the war on marijuana. Catching an opponent in an outright lie is the surest way to the mainstream. 

Letting the states set their own marijuana policies, and encouraging them to learn from the Dutch experience, would be entirely in the American mainstream. When this country was founded, Dutch religious tolerance was the model for the world, and it was an experience that the several states took to heart. That is about as mainstream as we can get.
